extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and psychology (readers of William James / radical empiricism)
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing and philosophically characterizing 'activity' as a feature of experience using pragmatic and radical-empiricist methods; distinguishing psychological, metaphysical, and logical questions about activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Pure Experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing shall be admitted as fact except what can be experienced at some definite time by some experient; for every feature of fact experienced, a definite place must be found somewhere in the final system of reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete, directly experienceable items as the basic data for theory; every posited kind of thing must be locatable in experience somewhere. The principle functions methodically: do not posit facts that cannot in principle be experienced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic Method for Meaning and Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no difference of truth that doesn't make a difference of fact somewhere; determine the meaning of differences of opinion by making the discussion hinge on some practical or particular issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims (especially metaphysical ones), ask what practical or observable difference would follow from accepting them. Require a concrete or practical consequence to ground abstract distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic Separation of Questions about Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish three separate questions: (1) psychological—Have we perceptions of activity? what are they like? (2) metaphysical—Is there a fact of activity? what idea must we frame of it? (3) logical—Whence do we know activity? by feeling alone or other sources?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep these three issues distinct in argument and description; avoid conflating descriptive phenomenology with metaphysical or epistemological claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/Criterion of Bare Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Bare activity (in the broadest sense) is any apprehension of something 'doing' — change taking place; a conjunctive object in experience that marks that something is going on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'bare activity' need not contain direction, actor, or aim. It is the basic experiential datum of change or happening, prior to specification of agent or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for Complex Activity-Situations (what counts as experienced 'activity')
rubrics_metrics.description: In complex experiences called activity-situations, activity appears with definite direction (tendency), desire or sense of goal, resistances, efforts (strain or squeeze), and where sustained, the appearance of will; outcomes include triumph or passive giving up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To count an experience as an activity-situation, identify the felt tendency, the felt obstacle, the felt effort/strain, and the felt outcome. These conjunctive ingredients constitute the experiential 'gestalt-qualitӓt' of activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of Authenticity for Experienced Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: An experiencer who possesses the feeling of tendency against felt obstacles, effort, and outcome possesses all that the idea of activity contains; the percipi in such originals of experience is the esse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When someone sincerely reports an experience of activity (tendency, struggle, overcoming or succumbing), that phenomenological report contains the essential content of 'activity' as an object of inquiry; do not dismiss felt activity as merely illusory without arguing what would replace its explanatory role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological Caution Against Endless Descriptive Cataloguing
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensive descriptive inventories of activity-situations may merely elaborate the obvious and risk never reaching substantive theoretical conclusions—the question 'where is it going to stop?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor descriptions that bear on theoretical or pragmatic consequences. Avoid interminable synonymic or picturesque catalogues of familiar experiences that add little to understanding or application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for Assessing 'Most Real' Agent in an Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: An onlooker with a wider field of vision regards the most previous agent ascertainable (the first source of action) as the most real agent; intermediate agents merely transmit that impulse and are assigned less 'reality' or responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assigning reality or responsibility among nested activities, identify the earliest ascertainable source whose cessation would stop the larger activity (causal priority). That agent should be treated as the primary real agent for purposes of explanation and blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology of Philosophical Accounts of 'Real' Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophical substitutes for immediately felt activities typically take three principal forms: (1) wider-spanned consciousness (a 'will' with broader time-span) as agent; (2) ideas in struggle as agents whose prevalence constitutes action; (3) nerve-cells and physiological processes as the true agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one posits any such substitute as the 'real' activity, one must show what practical or experiential consequences this substitution entails and how it differs from simply accepting the felt activity. Examine what the substitution 'practically involves.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for the Intelligibility of External Relations
rubrics_metrics.description: External (spatial, temporal, situational) relations can be intelligible without altering the inner nature of the terms; they are relations created 'pro hac vice' by casual situation and can change without forcing intrinsic changes in the relata.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims about relations by thought-experiment: can the relation change while the relata keep their intrinsic characters? If yes, treating the relation as external and intelligible is permissible. Do not assume that a relation 'must' be an internal alteration of the terms without demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for Understanding Conjunctions vs. Abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding a complex (conjunction AB) is achieved by seeing the concrete conjunction as given in experience; the intellect that only analyzes and isolates abstract A or B may fail to grasp their lived conjunction unless it accepts the experienced whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing complexes, prioritize the concrete experiential data of conjunctions (the 'fact as given') over demands for an abstract prefigured 'intelligible' union. Avoid presupposing an intellectual faculty that must pre-exist to 'join' parts before experience.
